references.text: The original instruction for making the horns on the burnt offering altar, as Exodus 38:2 describes their construction. The horns were to be made in one piece with the altar and crafted from bronze.
The incense altar also had horns on its four corners, reflecting the same design principle for horned altars in the tabernacle.
The altar's horns were used in sacrificial rituals, where the priest applied blood to them. This highlights the ritual significance of the horns described in Exodus 38:2.
The priest took blood from the sin offering and applied it to the horns of the burnt offering altar, illustrating the use of the horns as described in Exodus 38:2.
Adonijah seized hold of the altar's horns to seek refuge, demonstrating how the altar's horns functioned as a place of asylum.
A reference to the altar's horns in connection with the festival offering, showing the enduring significance of the altar's horns in Israel's worship.
Ezekiel's vision of the future altar also includes four horns, following the same pattern as the tabernacle's altar.
The altar's horns at Bethel are mentioned in connection with God's judgment, highlighting their importance in Israelite religious practice.
Highlights the shared structural and symbolic significance of the horns being integrated into both types of altars.
